title: A Ministry of Reconciliation: 2 Corinthians 5:18–6:2
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: Pastor Tito Lyro expounds on Paul's teaching that God has reconciled humanity to Himself through Jesus Christ and has given believers the ministry of proclaiming this reconciliation to the world. The sermon emphasizes that reconciliation is God's initiative alone, accomplished through Christ's finished work on the cross, and calls all people—whether believers, doubters, unbelievers, or hypocrites—to respond to this grace by faith.

outline.title: The Need for Reconciliation: Humanity's Separation from God
subpoints: Sin entered the world through Adam's disobedience and is passed to all humanity
All people are born as sinners and enemies of God, not seeking Him
The divide between humanity and God is total and requires God's initiative to bridge

outline.title: The Instrument of Reconciliation: God's Work Through Christ
subpoints: God reconciled the world to Himself through Jesus Christ at the cross
Reconciliation is accomplished, not partial—Christ said 'It is finished'
God did not impute our trespasses to us because Christ bore our guilt
All kinds of people from every ethnicity and background can be reconciled through Christ

outline.title: The Message of Reconciliation: The Gospel Proclaimed
subpoints: Paul and all gospel ministers are ambassadors for Christ speaking God's word
The command to be reconciled to God is issued through faith in Christ
The grace of God must not be received in vain—it demands a response of faith
Christ is the only mediator between God and humanity

outline.title: The Call to Reconciliation: Applications to Different Believers
subpoints: True believers are called to rest in Christ's completed work and live in peace
Weak believers should trust in Christ's strength, not their own faith
Doubting believers must believe God's declaration over their feelings
Unbelievers in the congregation must repent and believe the gospel
Hypocrites must stop pretending and be genuinely reconciled to God
Married believers should reflect God's reconciliation in their marriages
Single believers should find their identity and security in union with Christ
Covenant children must personally embrace Christ rather than presume upon their upbringing

outline.title: The Historical Context: Grace and Restoration
subpoints: The surrender at Appomattox Courthouse illustrates God's gracious restoration of enemies
Grant's refusal to celebrate and his provision for Confederate soldiers mirrors God's mercy
Unlike earthly reconciliation, God alone took the initiative to make peace with rebels

transcript:
## Scripture Reading

> Now all things are of God who has reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ and has given us the ministry of reconciliation, that is that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not imputing their trespasses to them, and has committed to us the Word of reconciliation. Now then we are ambassadors for Christ as though God were pleading through us. We implore you on Christ's behalf be reconciled to God, for He made Him who knew no sin to be sinned for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him. We then as workers together with Him also plead with you not to receive the grace of God in vain, for He says, in an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. Behold now is the accepted time, behold now is the day of salvation. (2 Corinthians 5:18–6:2)

## The Picture of Reconciliation: Appomattox Courthouse

In April of 1865, after four years of the bloodiest war in American history, the Confederate army under General Robert E. Lee surrendered to the Union army under Ulysses S. Grant at the Appomattox Courthouse. The nation had been torn apart; more than 600,000 soldiers had died in the bloodiest war that the United States has ever been involved in. There was bitterness, there was hatred, there was suspicion on both sides.

Yet after the surrender, Grant did something very remarkable. He would not allow his men to celebrate the Confederates' surrender. He ordered that no salutes be fired because he said the Confederates are now our countrymen. He also permitted Lee's starving, hungry soldiers to keep their horses so that they could ride home and plant their crops in the spring so that they could feed their families.

Why did he do that? Because in that moment, war was over. The enemies were not merely defeated; they were being restored to fellowship in one nation again. Reconciliation had taken place.

That is a faint picture of what Paul is describing in 2 Corinthians 5. Sin has made us enemies of God, but unlike Appomattox, where both sides laid down their arms, in our reconciliation with God, the initiative comes entirely from one side. We're still His enemies, and God Himself came seeking peace. He sent His Son who bore our guilt on the cross, and now He sends His ambassadors into the world with this astonishing message: be reconciled to God.

The gospel is God's apologist proclamation to rebels. We are the rebels. The war has been ended by Christ. The terms of peace have been secured at the cross. And now the King's ambassadors plead with sinners everywhere: be reconciled to God. That's what we see in this passage.

## The Need for Reconciliation

### The Fact of Separation

If you look at verses 18 and 19, what you see there is the need and then the instrument of reconciliation—what God uses to reconcile us to Himself. This whole passage assumes the need for reconciliation between man and God. Even though Paul does not expressly state it with a verse saying that you have not been reconciled, the fact that we need reconciliation tells us that we have been separated from God.

The reconciliation between man and God is necessary because they have been separated, and there's a great divide between humanity and God. This divide was created when Adam disobeyed God in the Garden of Eden.

### The Source: Adam's Sin

God created Adam and Eve. Adam stood as our representative before God. In him we were united. We read this in Genesis chapter 3, verses 6 and 7, and then 24:

> So when the woman—that's Eve—saw that the tree was good for food, that it was pleasant to the eyes and a tree desirable to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate. She also gave to her husband with her and he ate. Then the eyes of both of them were open and they knew that they were naked and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves coverings. And therefore the Lord God sent him out of the Garden of Eden to till the ground from which he was taken. (Genesis 3:6-7, 24)

Paul saw that truth means that we all sinned in that sin of Adam. In Romans chapter 5, verse 12, Paul says:

> Therefore, just as through one man sin entered the world and death through sin and thus death spread to all men because all sinned. (Romans 5:12)

Again in verse 18 of Romans 5, Paul says:

> Therefore, as through one man's offense judgment came to all men resulting in condemnation. Whereas by one man's disobedience many were made sinners. (Romans 5:18)

So we're separated from God because of the sin of our forefather Adam, which is counted as ours. We are polluted by that sin—that is, we have a nature that is inclined away from God, a sinful nature. We are guilty of that sin, but that divide continues because we sin ourselves. It's not just that Adam did it and we get mad at Adam; we practice sinning as well.

Remember what Romans 3:23 says:

> For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. (Romans 3:23)

In Galatians 3:23, Paul says:

> The scripture has confined all under sin. (Galatians 3:23)

### All Are Enemies of God

The Bible describes all peoples apart from Christ as being enemies of God. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, there was the seeker-friendly movement where the church was supposed to conform to those who were seeking God. Well, according to the scriptures, there's no one who seeks God. According to the scriptures, they are all enemies of God.

Romans 5, verses 6, 8, and 10 read this way:

> When we were still without strength in due time Christ died for the ungodly. But God demonstrated His own love towards us in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us. For if when we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more having been reconciled we shall be saved by His life. (Romans 5:6, 8, 10)

We were without strength, we were sinners, we were enemies. That's where God met us—not when we were seeking Him, not when we were doing great things for His cause.

Paul affirms in Colossians 1:21:

> You who once were alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works yet now He has reconciled. (Colossians 1:21)

Notice that in all these descriptions of separation, the sinner doesn't move toward God, but rather God moves toward the sinner. God finds you where you are and brings you to Himself. God is in the business of reconciling all people to Himself.

## The Instrument of Reconciliation: God's Work

### All Things Belong to God

That's why He says in verse 18:

> Now all things are of God who has reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ and has given us the ministry of reconciliation. (2 Corinthians 5:18)

All things—all things absolutely belong to God. They proceed from God, they exist for God. But the all things that Paul is talking about here is all things pertaining to reconciliation between God and man. It doesn't belong to somebody else; it doesn't belong to you; it belongs to God who is reconciling all peoples to Himself.

All things pertaining to the entirety of salvation—from regeneration, or the new birth, to glorification at the return of Christ—all belong to God and to His grace.

### God's Reconciliation Through Christ

Paul not only knows cognitively that God reconciles man to Himself, but he also knows experientially because in verse 18, Paul says that God has reconciled him to Himself. Remember, the "we's" and the "us" throughout this passage refer primarily to Paul and Timothy in their apostolic office.

Paul was one who had persecuted Christ Himself by persecuting His church. Yet he was reconciled to God through the same Christ he sought to destroy. The one he wanted to destroy, in His kindness and grace, reached down to Paul and brought him to Himself.

Remember the story in Acts chapter 9, verses 1 through 6. Paul, back then called Saul, was breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord. Luke, who wrote Acts, says:

> Then Saul still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord went to the high priest and asked letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus so that if he found any who were of the way, whether man or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. (Acts 9:1-2)

Paul wanted to destroy the church; that was his goal. He wanted to bring anyone—any Jew who confessed Christ—to Jerusalem to be tried and stoned. But Luke continues:

> As he journeyed he came near Damascus and suddenly a light shone around him from heaven. Then he fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?" And he said, "Who are You, Lord?" Then the Lord said, "I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. It is hard for you to kick against the goads." So he, Paul, trembling and astonished said, "Lord, Master, the one who now owns me, what do you want me to do?" (Acts 9:3-6)

What a transformation! That's an awesome thing that happens in the life of the believer. And then on top of that, God, after reconciling Paul to Himself through His Son Jesus Christ, gave him the ministry of reconciliation. He's on the way to Damascus to go kill Christians, and then God says, "You're Mine now. You reconcile it to Me, and now your life is going to be spent telling others about this Christ that reconciles people to Myself."

Paul, who worked so hard to destroy Christ, is now called to take the message of reconciliation to the world. What a merciful, good, and compassionate God that we have and that we serve.

## The Message of Reconciliation

### What Is the Ministry of Reconciliation?

Now, what is the ministry or the message of reconciliation that God gave to Paul? We find that in verse 19:

> That is that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself not imputing their trespasses to them and has committed to us the word of reconciliation. (2 Corinthians 5:19)

The message, the ministry of reconciliation is that God reconciled the world to Himself through the cross of Christ. What a big and encouraging message! And I want you to notice that it says He has done it. He has done it. He doesn't have to do it anymore. He has done it. The world is reconciled to Christ.

Now, if you were a Greek student, you would notice that the word "world" here is used without the article. In English it says "the world," but in the original language, Greek, it's just "world"—no article. This means that Paul was referring to the quality, not the quantity. Paul's not saying that Christ, God in Christ, is reconciling everybody who has ever lived or everybody who's living today to Christ, but that God in Christ has reconciled all kinds of people to Himself. It's not just Jews, but it's all ethnic groups.

When John has a vision of heaven in the book of Revelation, he says:

> There is a multitude that cannot be numbered and they come from every tribe, from every language, from every color, from every clan, from every speech, from every language before the Lamb who was once slain and now lives. (Revelation 7:9)

No matter what kind of person you are, you can be reconciled to God through the cross of Christ. So Paul says in 2 Timothy 2:5-6:

> There is one God and there is only one mediator between God and man, the man Jesus Christ, who gave Himself a ransom for all to be testified. (2 Timothy 2:5-6)

Friends, there's only one way to God, and that is through the Lord Jesus Christ. No matter who you are, no matter where you are, no matter what kind of person you are, it's through Christ, who is the mediator—the one that mediates, that brings you to the Father. That's the only way of reconciliation.

### The Work Is Finished

I think it's important that in verse 19, you notice that Paul says that God "was reconciling" the world to Himself through Christ. This past tense "was" refers to the cross of Christ. Reconciliation has been accomplished completely in the cross of Christ.

Christ really meant it when on the cross He said, "It is finished." It's not kind of finished. It's not mostly finished. It is finished.

### The Means of Reconciliation: Not Imputing Sins

You notice also how Paul describes the ministry of reconciliation—he describes it in two parts. God was reconciling the world to Himself through the cross of Christ. The means of reconciliation is not counting your guilt as yours. Not imputing their trespasses to themselves: if you're in Christ, God the Father did not count all your sins as yours. He chose not to. Why can He do that? Because:

> He who knew no sin became guilty of sin that we may be made the righteousness of God. (2 Corinthians 5:21)

The cross of Christ secures your reconciliation to the Father. Quoting Psalm 32, Paul in Romans 4:7-8 says:

> Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord shall not impute sin. (Romans 4:7-8)

This morning in the responsive reading, we read Psalm 130:

> If You, Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? (Psalm 130:3)

Can you imagine if God held every one of us to our sins? And yet the psalmist says:

> There is forgiveness with You that You may be feared. (Psalm 130:4)

God has committed to Paul the Word of reconciliation. Now this begs the question: What is the Word of reconciliation?

Well, the Word of reconciliation is the gospel of Jesus Christ. For the message, Paul says in 1 Corinthians 1:18:

> The message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. (1 Corinthians 1:18)

To those who don't believe, if you're here and you're not believing in Christ, you think that what we're doing here is just stupid. It's foolishness. And yet it is that Word that reconciles you. It's that message: that the sinless One became sin on the cross for you, that you might be the righteousness of God. That reconciles you to God.

All that needed to be done for all kinds of people to be reconciled to God has already been done, and that's been done on the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ. Now it needs to be appropriated by faith.

## The Call to Reconciliation

### The Command to Be Reconciled

So Paul pleads with the Corinthians for them to be reconciled to God. Look at verse 20:

> Now then we are ambassadors for Christ as though God were pleading through us. We implore you on Christ's behalf be reconciled to God. (2 Corinthians 5:20)

And look at verses 1 and 2 of chapter 6:

> We then as workers together with Him also plead with you not to receive the grace of God in vain, for He says, "In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you." Behold now is the accepted time, behold now is the day of salvation. (2 Corinthians 6:1-2)

Paul as an ambassador and minister of the gospel, Paul as an apostle and minister of the gospel, is an ambassador for the Word of God. You know what an ambassador is, right? An ambassador is one who speaks for the ruler. And when the ambassador speaks, the one whom he represents speaks through him. When a minister of the gospel speaks according to the scriptures, it is Christ speaking to you.

Here Paul says—rather, Christ says—"Be reconciled to God." It's a command. It's not something that you should decide whether to do or not. You be reconciled to God through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

### Why Call the Church to Be Reconciled?

Now, as I was reading this, a question came to my mind: Why is Paul calling the Corinthians to be reconciled to God when he already called them the church of God and the saints in Corinth? Why is he calling church people to be reconciled to God?

Well, one part of the answer is because the visible church—us—we are a mixed group. Remember the parable of the wheat and the tares in Matthew 13:24? Jesus says:

> The kingdom of heaven is like a field that is planted, and the wheat comes, but then the enemy comes and spreads the weeds, and the weeds and the wheat look alike. So He doesn't want the servants to pull in the weeds in case they pull the wheat out as well. (Matthew 13:24)

That's us. That's the church. We are a mixed bag. So we need to constantly be calling people to come to faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Another part of the answer is that those who are already reconciled to God through the cross of Christ need to lean further into the fact that we are reconciled to God because we forget. Although Protestant theology denies that penance is required—that we have to do things for God to forgive us—we often relate to God in that way. We ignore that Christ has indeed paid it all, and all to Him we owe, and try to do acts of penance as if God was not satisfied with His Son.

But friends, when Paul calls people to reconciliation, that's what he's doing. That's why Paul—or I, or anyone who proclaims the gospel of Jesus—can implore the world to be reconciled with God: because Christ, who knew no sin, became guilty of sin, so that we can become the righteousness of God.

In verse 20 of chapter 5, Paul says he's a fellow worker with Christ. And as such, he begs the Corinthians not to receive the grace of God in vain. See that in verse 1 of chapter 6:

> And as your minister I plead with you not to receive the grace of God in vain. (2 Corinthians 6:1)

These are church people that Paul is talking to. These are church people to whom Paul is ministering. They have heard the gospel preached a thousand times. They have participated in the sacraments. They have been prayed for. They have fellowship with the saints, the same as with us. And you have received that over and over and over and over again. And yet you are not embracing it by faith. The grace that God has bestowed upon you—so I plead with you, don't waste any of that. Today is the day. Right now is the time of salvation. Don't play around with the grace of God as if it were an empty thing.

## Eight Applications for Different Believers

As we come towards the end of our time here, how does the command to be reconciled to God apply to all the different segments of the church? I want to give you eight brief applications.

### 1. To the True Believer

First, I want to talk to you, brother and sister, who is the true believer. The call here is to rest in the reconciliation that Christ has already secured for you. You are not being asked to reconcile yourself to God or to earn His favor again. Rather, you are being called to live in peace—in the peace that Christ purchased for you.

Stop trying to pay for your sins because Christ has already paid for them. Draw near to God with confidence. Live as one who is no longer God's enemy, but His child. So rejoice, rejoice in your acceptance before God, and pursue holiness out of gratitude.

### 2. To the Weak Believer

To the weak believer, the call is to not measure God's reconciliation by the strength of your faith. Weak faith still lays hold of a strong Savior, and that's what matters. Now a Christian may say, "My faith is small, or I struggle with assurance, or I still battle sin." Yet Paul says God has reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ.

Brothers and sisters, the ground of reconciliation is Christ's finished work, not the vigor of your faith. So look away from yourself back to Christ.

### 3. To the Doubting Believer

Thirdly, to the doubting believer, the call here is to believe God's declaration more than your feelings. Believe God's declaration more than your feelings. Many doubting Christians think, "Perhaps God is still angry with me," or "Perhaps I have sinned too much."

But reconciliation means the enmity has been gone. Remember what Romans 8:1 says:

> There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. (Romans 8:1)

So receive anew the peace of God in Christ Jesus.

### 4. To the Unbeliever in the Congregation

Four: To the unbeliever in the congregation, the call is straightforward: Repent and believe the gospel. Repent and believe the gospel. You may attend church. You may know Christian doctrine and even admire Christ, yet you remain unreconciled. The ambassador of Christ says, "Lay down your arms. Flee to Christ. Receive the reconciliation He freely offers. Today is a day to come to Christ."

### 5. To the Hypocrite

Five: To the hypocrite in our midst—this perhaps is the sharpest application. You may possess church membership. You may possess theological knowledge. You may possess an outwardly moral life, and yet you may still be in enmity with God. The call is for you to stop pretending. Stop pretending. Be genuinely reconciled to God because external religion cannot do anything for you. Only Christ can.

### 6. To the Married Believer

Six: To the married believer, the call is to live out horizontally with your spouse a life of reconciliation that has already happened vertically between you and your God. That's what marriage should reflect. Marriage should reflect the peace that God has made with us. So husband, wife, put away bitterness. There's no place for bitterness in our marriages. Forgive as you've been forgiven, and pursue peace in the home.

### 7. To the Single Believer

Seven: To the single believer, the call is just this: Your deepest identity is not in marriage, but in your reconciliation with God. You are not incomplete because you are unmarried. Your greatest relationship has already been secured through Christ. So find your contentment and security in union with Christ.

### 8. To Covenant Children

And lastly, number eight: To our covenant children, the call to you is that the God of your parents calls you to embrace Christ for yourself. You enjoy great privileges in the covenant community, but you must personally trust in Christ. Do not presume upon your upbringing. Believe in the Lord Jesus. Make Him your own Savior.

## The Final Call

At the end of the day, though, there are only two groups of people in this room today: those who are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ and those who remain His enemies. But the glory of the gospel is that God has made peace possible through the cross of His Son.

The war is over for all who are in Christ. The debt has been paid. The righteousness has been provided. The invitation is still being extended.

So brothers, so friends, so sisters: If you're a believer, rest—rest in the reconciliation Christ has secured for you. Live as one who is at peace with God. And if you're not yet reconciled to Him, do not delay. Paul says, "Today, today is the accepted time. Today is the day of salvation."

Here, hear the plea of the King again through His ambassador: Be reconciled to God. When you leave this place today, do not leave merely having heard about reconciliation. Leave here having been reconciled to Christ. Respond to His grace that He has towards you in Christ.
